**Australian Public Service — 7,600 public servants discover that the brief is the product (2024)**

Between January and June 2024, Australia's Digital Transformation Agency ran a whole-of-government trial of Microsoft 365 Copilot: more than 7,600 staff across over 60 federal agencies, all handed the same tool at the same time. Unusually, the government published the full evaluation rather than a press release.

The warm numbers were there. The DTA reported that 86 per cent of participants wanted to keep using Copilot and 69 per cent said tasks were faster. Sitting underneath was a more honest finding: 39 per cent did not think it improved the quality of their work, and only about a third used it daily. Same licence, same software, wildly different experiences.

The evaluation was direct about why. Focus-group participants described prompting as one of the steepest learning curves and said it was not a widely held skill in the public service — it took training and repeated experimentation. Staff who tailored prompts to specify style, tone and format got output that fitted the job; without that, Copilot returned generic, contextually unaware responses. The variable was not the technology. It was the brief.

That is this lesson, tested on 7,600 people. You are about to write two versions of the same request — one queried like a search box, one briefed like a colleague — and watch the gap open up. The public servants who got value were not the technical ones. They were the ones who said who the output was for, what tone it needed and what "good" looked like, before they pressed enter.

**Citizens Advice — the assistant that was only allowed to know one thing (2024–2025)**

Advisers at Citizens Advice answer questions about benefits, debt, housing and employment — areas where the rules shift and a confident wrong answer does real harm. When the charity's Stockport, Oldham, Rochdale and Trafford offices worked with the UK government's AI incubator on an assistant called Caddy, the design decision that mattered was a restriction. Caddy drafts its answers from Citizens Advice's own public and internal guidance and hands back the links, rather than writing from whatever it absorbed during training.

In effect they took the idea at the heart of this lesson and built a machine out of it. The model can only work with what is placed in front of it, so they placed the right material there — and nothing else. A supervisor still reviews the suggestion before anything reaches a client, and the charity deliberately pointed the tool at its advisers rather than the public.

A randomised controlled trial embedded in live operations, covering more than 1,000 support interactions, sent questions either to Caddy or to a human supervisor. Advisers with access to Caddy were reported to be twice as likely to feel confident in the advice they gave, and 1.5 times more likely to resolve the client's issue.

Your version takes ten seconds and no build team. Pasting the actual policy, the actual email thread, the actual meeting notes into the chat is the same move: filling the context window with the thing that matters, so the model stops guessing. That is precisely what this lesson asks you to practise.

**Swindon Borough Council — the blade nobody in the building had reached for (2023–2024)**

Councils are expected to offer Easy Read versions of important documents — care plans, benefits letters, consultations — for residents with learning disabilities: short sentences, large text, supporting pictures. Producing them was slow and costly. Swindon Borough Council said a standard Easy Read service worked out at around £120 an A4 page, which put a proper version of anything long out of reach for everyday correspondence.

In late 2023 the council built Simply Readable, an in-house tool that takes a dense document and returns an Easy Read draft. Swindon reported a cost of under 10 pence a page, with social workers able to put complex information in and get a usable version back in under half an hour. It was co-created with residents who have learning disabilities — the council's "experts by experience" — who shaped what the format actually needed to do. Swindon then released it open source and licence-free, and Edinburgh, Newport, Southampton and West Berkshire picked it up.

The striking part is not the technology. It is the capability nobody had thought to reach for. Plenty of those staff already had an assistant that could rewrite text for a named audience. Rewriting for an audience had never occurred to anyone as a thing to ask for.

That is the risk this lesson exists to remove. You are about to write a working mini-prompt for a blade you have never used — critique, role-play, comparison, translating for a reader who is not you. Swindon's whole innovation was noticing that one was there.

**Morgan & Morgan — eight of the nine cases did not exist (2025)**

In January 2025, lawyers acting for a family suing Walmart over an allegedly defective hoverboard filed pre-trial motions in a federal court in Wyoming. The motions cited nine cases. Eight of them were not real. They had come out of an AI tool the firm used internally, and they looked exactly like genuine citations — correct format, plausible names, confident supporting passages.

Walmart's lawyers checked them. So did the court. In a 24 February 2025 order, US District Judge Kelly Rankin sanctioned three lawyers a total of $5,000, removed the associate who had drafted the motions from the case, and set out the duty plainly: a lawyer must read the case to confirm that the passage they are relying on is existing law. Morgan & Morgan is one of the largest firms in the United States, and it followed up with an email to its more than 1,000 lawyers warning that filing invented case law could cost them their job.

Nobody involved was careless about the law. They were careless about one step: opening the source. The entire failure sits in the gap between "this looks right" and "I checked".

Your version of that gap is far smaller and far cheaper to close. A statistic in a board paper, a date in a client email, a policy line you have quoted back to someone, a total at the bottom of a column. None of it calls for fear of the tool — it calls for a minute. Anything carrying a name, number, date, quote or link gets opened before you rely on it.

**Commonwealth of Pennsylvania — 95 minutes a day, found in the dullest work in the building (2024–2025)**

From March 2024 to March 2025, Pennsylvania's Office of Administration ran a generative-AI pilot with around 175 state employees across 14 agencies — HR officers, IT staff, policy and programme people — and published what it learned in a report the following month.

The headline the state reported was an average of 95 minutes saved a day, with 85 per cent of participants describing a positive experience. The more useful part is where that time came from. Nothing visionary: rewriting job descriptions into plain language, which the state said helped bring hiring and onboarding down from about 90 days to 60; and a team pulling 93 tangled IT policies into 34. Drafting, summarising, tidying, comparing. The unglamorous middle of everybody's week.

The report was careful not to oversell it. It said the assistant is no substitute for the judgement and experience staff bring, and listed real barriers — worries about accuracy, and the time it takes to learn to use the thing well. Pennsylvania later opened access to more than 3,000 employees across 35 agencies.

You are not running a state pilot. But the shape of the win is identical, and it is the one you are about to build: a recurring, low-stakes task with raw material you can paste in, a fully briefed prompt, one round of iteration, then a check of the names, numbers and dates. Pick the dullest repeating job in your week. That is where your 95 minutes are hiding.
